I met a temp laborer on monday that I suspect has this. Any tips on dealing with them?
Anyone here have friends that have aspergers?

I think one important thing is you should not expect them to read your mind, spell things out (but try to not be condescending). This is even more important when it comes to social stuff.

Oh, and if they end up saying or doing something you or a coworker consider offensive, try to first explain to them (the asperger person) why from your perspective it is considered offensive before assuming they meant to offend.

or better yet assume they know and check your offended privilege.

Have you explained to any number of people in the last 12 months that they are being offensive? If the answer is yes then you're a shitlord pushing your triggered offendedness privilege.

For some aspies, the whole world seems to be triggerhappy.

If you're not dealing with extremists, it is possible to reach an acceptable compromise on both sides; but you need to be willing not only to talk, but to listen as well.

People on the spectrum at the higher end have an inherent dislike of falsehood (it's a social thing that remains under developed) many of the compromises and tweaks in common conversation involve euphemisms, lies by omission, or outright lies. This is one of the reasons regular people can sometimes irritate them so much. One of the things that's draining about interacting with regular people is the constant need to engage in lies and intrigue in order to be considered polite. Whereas in fact these demands are outrageous in their own right.

People never seem to look at it that way though.

Partly it's a communication and behavior gap. Things that might come naturally to you may not come naturally to him and so on.

One common issue is eye contact. Not just that it's difficult to maintain, but that it's difficult to judge how long to look, when to look, when to look away. People have this entire layer of unconscious communication that can be difficult or distracting to someone with Asperger's. Not maintaining eye contact can be a way of hitting the mute button on that feedback and focusing more directly on what the speaker is saying.

I dated a girl with Aspergers. Big things where never use sarcasm, don't get offended by anything they say if it is offensive they don't mean for it to be, and just straight up tell them what you want done and how you want it done.

Big Sur off the Bucket List

Very Late Race Report:

The good:

  • The course is even more beautiful than the pictures. The scenery is spectacular from start to finish. It truly lives up to the hype.

  • The people running are all runners. Nothing against the first timer, bucket list types, but it was kinda cool being around so many dedicated runners. The older lady (70s) that I was talking with before the race, for example....she'd done Dopey earlier this year too. When I showed surprise, she mentioned it was only tough because she had to run through food poisoning, but the ironman training helped out. yeah........

  • Piano guy and the other randoms out there. In the middle of stunning waves and rocks, you start hearing classical music floating through the air, or drums bouncing off the cliffs and surrounding hills. It adds to keep the run from being just a beautiful run.

The okay:

  • goddamn wind. Uphill for miles and 25+ mph wind. We all could've done without that.

  • Traffic after the race. You finish in a small town with one road in and one road out....the road that happens to be the one everybody is running on. The crew was great and broke everything down quickly, but the traffic jam was inevitable. And it sucked.

Overall:

  • I will sign up every year for as long as I run. I'm toying with the idea of hitting a race in every state, but will take Big Sur over a new state every time I'm lucky enough to have my name pulled.
